name: Enter a GitHub release

input.query: INSERT INTO models (owner_id, game_id, version, repo, release_tag) SELECT ($1)::uuid, g.id, coalesce(max(m.version), 0) + 1, ($3)::text, ($4)::text FROM games g LEFT JOIN models m ON m.owner_id = ($1)::uuid AND m.game_id = g.id WHERE g.slug = ($2)::text GROUP BY g.id

SELECT json_build_object('model_id', m.id, 'version', m.version, 'status', m.status)::text AS body FROM models m JOIN games g ON g.id = m.game_id WHERE m.owner_id = ($1)::uuid AND g.slug = ($2)::text   AND m.repo = ($3)::text AND m.release_tag = ($4)::text

description: Two statements, not one: db_write returns only rows_affected, so the row is read back. The one-in-flight and duplicate-release rules are partial unique indexes; since Orion 1.5.0 a violation is classified as integrity_unique and answers 409 CONFLICT on its own, so no task catches it -- the run halts at the insert and the platform states the conflict. The two indexes are indistinguishable to the workflow by design (the constraint name is not surfaced), which is fine here: the scope asks for 409 either way. See orion-gaps.md G2. The body column is cast to text and parsed back by a parse_json task: Orion's db_read goes through sqlx's Any driver, which cannot decode the Postgres json/jsonb type and fails the task outright. Casting keeps response construction in SQL -- see README 'Postgres builds the response JSON' -- at the cost of one extra task.
